His saying, the Exalted: {إِلاَّ مَنْ أَمَرَ}: about this exception there are two views: the first, that it is continuous; the second, that it is discontinuous; and both are based on whether «النجوى» may mean the maṣdar, like «الدَّعْوى», in which case it has the meaning of secret conversing (tanājī), or may mean the people who converse secretly, applying the maṣdar to what occurs from it figuratively, as in «رجلٌ عَدْل وصَوْم». On the first it is discontinuous, because the one who commands is not a conversing, so it is as if it were said: "but whoever commands charity — in his secret conversation there is good". The Kufans imply the discontinuous exception with «بل», and some made the exception continuous even if the maṣdar is meant by «النجوى», and that is by omitting a muḍāf, as if it were said "except the secret talk of one who commands"; and if we make «النجوى» mean the secret converser, it is continuous. You know from what has preceded that the discontinuous is always accusative in the dialect of the Hijaz, that the Banū Tamīm treat it like the continuous provided that the governor can be directed toward it, and that when the sentence is a negation or resembles one, the excepted may follow as a badal, which is the preferred, or be accusative in the basic manner of the exception. So His saying {إِلاَّ مَنْ أَمَرَ} is either accusative as a discontinuous exception if you take it as discontinuous in the dialect of the Hijaz, or accusative in the basic exception if you take it as continuous, or genitive as a badal from «كثير» or from «نجواهم», or an adjective of one of the two: as you say, «لا تَمُرَّ بجماعة من القوم إلا زيد» — if you wish you may make Zayd a follower of the group or of the people. Al-Zamakhsharī made it a follower only of «كثير». He said: "«إلا نَجْوَى مَنْ أمر» on the basis that it is genitive, a badal from «كثير», as you say «لا خيرَ في قيامِهم إلا قيامِ زيدٍ»"; and in illustration by this example there is a consideration, the dissimilarity of which to the verse is not hidden. All this holds if we take the exception to be continuous in the two interpretations mentioned, or discontinuous in the dialect of Tamīm. Six possibilities are summarised in it: the accusative as discontinuous in the dialect of the Hijaz, or in the basic exception; and the genitive as a badal from «كثير» or from «نجواهم», or as an adjective of one of the two.
And {مِّن نَّجْوَاهُمْ}: attached to an omitted word because it is an adjective of «كثير», so it is in the position of the genitive. «النجوى» in origin is a maṣdar as was stated, and it may be applied to persons figuratively [He the Exalted said: {وَإِذْ هُمْ نجوى} [al-Isrāʾ: 47]]; its meaning is secret speaking, and it occurs only between two or more. Al-Zajjāj said: "«النجوى» is what two or more are alone in, whether secret or open." It was also said: «النجوى» is the plural of «نَجِيّ»; al-Karmānī reported it. His saying «بين» may be accusative by «إصلاح» itself, as you say «أصلحت بين القوم»; He the Exalted said: {فَأَصْلِحُواْ بَيْنَ أَخَوَيْكُمْ} [al-Ḥujurāt: 10].
And it may be attached to an omitted word, as an adjective of «إصلاح», and «ابتغاءَ» is an object of purpose. The alif of «مرضاة» is from a wāw, and its verification has been given. Abū ʿAmr and Ḥamza read «فسوف يُؤتيه» with the yāʾ, looking to the overt noun in His saying {مَرْضَاتِ الله}, while the rest read it with the nūn, looking to His later saying «نُولِّه ونُصْلِه», which is more fitting for magnification.

semin-durr:115-115.t: {وَمَن يُشَاقِقِ}: it has been stated that the jussive imperfect and the imperative of the like of «لم يَرْدُدْ» and «رَدَّ» admit assimilation and leaving it, with details about that and the dialectal forms in it, in Āl ʿImrān; and likewise the ruling of the hāʾ in His saying «نُؤْته» and «نُصْلِه». And His saying {إِنَّ الله لاَ يَغْفِرُ أَن يُشْرَكَ بِهِ} [al-Nisāʾ: 48] has been given. That one (verse 48) was ended with His saying «فقد افترى» and this one with His saying «فقد ضَلَّ» because that is of the utmost appropriateness: the first is about the People of the Book, in that they have knowledge of the soundness of its establishment and that his law abrogates all laws, and despite that they were obstinate about it and so fabricated lies about Allah the Exalted; whereas this one is about polytheist people who are neither People of the Book nor possessors of knowledge, so describing them with error is fitting; moreover, guidance has been mentioned earlier, and it is the opposite of error.

semin-durr:117-117.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِلاَّ إِنَاثاً}: in this word there are nine readings. The well-known one, which is the plural of «أُنْثى», like «رِباب», the plural of «رُبّى». The second: al-Ḥasan read «أنثى» in the singular, and the plural is meant by it. The third — read by Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Ḥaywa, ʿAṭāʾ, also al-Ḥasan, Muʿādh al-Qārī, Abū al-ʿĀliya and Abū Nahīk: «إلا أُنُثا» like «رُسُل», and it has three possibilities. The first — and Ibn Jarīr said this — is that it is the plural of «إناث», like «ثِمار» and «ثُمُر», and «إناث» is the plural of «أنثى», so it is a plural of a plural, which is anomalous according to the grammarians. The second: it is the plural of «أنيث», like «قليب» and «قُلُب», «غدير» and «غُدُر»; «الأنيث» among men is the effeminate, weak one, and from it are «سيف أنيث وميناث وميناثة», i.e. a sword that does not cut. Ṣakhr said:
165 - 1- فتخْبِرَه بأنَّ العقلَ عندي ... جُرازٌ لا أَفَلُّ ولا أَنيثُ
(So you tell him that the intellect in my possession is a sharp sword, not notched and not blunt.)
The third: it is singular, i.e. it is one of the adjectives that came on the pattern fuʿul, like «امرأة حُنُثٌ». The fourth — read by Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Ibn ʿUmar and Abū al-Jawzāʾ — «وثَنا» with fatḥa on the wāw and the thāʾ, as a singular by which the plural is meant. The fifth — read by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, Muslim ibn Jundub, and also Ibn ʿAbbās — «أُثُنا» with ḍamma on the hamza and the thāʾ, and it has two possibilities, the more apparent of which is that it is the plural of «وثَن», like «أسَد» and «أُسُد»; then the wāw was changed to hamza because of its being given a necessary ḍamma, the original being «وُثُن», then «أُثُن». The second: that the singular «وَثَناً» was pluralised as «وِثان», like «جَمَل» and «جِمال», «جَبَل» and «جِبال»; then «وِثان» was pluralised as «وُثُن», like «حِمار» and «حُمُر»; then the wāw was changed into hamza for the reason given earlier, so it is a plural of a plural. Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejected this possibility, arguing that fiʿāl is a plural of abundance (jamʿ kathra), and plurals of abundance are not pluralised a second time; only those plurals are pluralised that are plurals of paucity (jamʿ qilla). There is an objection to this, in that a plural is not pluralised except anomalously, whether it is a plural of paucity or of anything else. The sixth — read by Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī: «وُثُنا», which is the origin of the reading before it. The seventh and eighth: «أُثْنا» and «وُثْنا» with sukūn on the thāʾ, with the hamza and the wāw, which are the lightening of fuʿul, like «سُقُف». The ninth — read by Abū al-Sawār, and so it was found in the codex of ʿĀʾisha: «إلا أَوْثاناً», the plural of «وَثَن», like «جَمَل» and «أَجْمال», «جَبَل» and «أَجْبال». Their idols were called "females" because they used to clothe them in kinds of ornament and name them with names of females, like al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt. This has been rejected, in that they were also named with names of males, such as Hubal and Dhū al-Khalaṣa, and there is a consideration in this, because the predominant practice was naming them with names of females. And «مريداً» is a faʿīl form from «مَرَدَ», i.e. he stripped himself bare for evil; from it «شجرة مَرْداء», i.e. its leaves have fallen; from it also «الأمْرَدُ», for his face being stripped of hair; and «الصَّرْحُ الممرَّد», on which no dust rises, is from the same.
Abū Rajāʾ read — and it is narrated from ʿĀṣim — «تدْعُون» in the second person.
His saying: {لَّعَنَهُ الله}: it has two possibilities. The more apparent is that the clause is an adjective of «شيطاناً», so it is in the position of the accusative. The second: it is resumptive, either as a report of that or as a supplication against him. And His saying «وقال» has three possibilities: also an adjective, or a ḥāl with «قد» implied, i.e. «وقد قال», or resumptive. And «لأتَّخِذَنَّ» is the answer to an omitted oath. And «من عبادك» may be attached to the verb before it or to an omitted word as a ḥāl from «نصيباً», because in origin it is an adjective of an indefinite noun put before it.

semin-durr:119-119.t:
The objects of the three verbs are omitted because they are indicated, i.e. "and I will lead them astray from guidance, and I will give them false hopes of falsehood, and I will command them to error", so Abū al-Baqāʾ implied it; but better is to imply the omitted from the same kind as the one expressed, i.e. «ولآمُرَنَّهم بالبَتك» ("I will command them to slit") and «ولآمُرَنّهم بالتغيير» ("I will command them to alter"). Abū ʿAmr read, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported from him, «ولامُرَنَّهم» without an alif, which is an anomalous shortening upon which no analogy is made. It is also permissible that nothing of that be implied, because the aim is to report the occurrence of these acts without regard to what they are attached to, like {كُلُواْ واشربوا} [al-Ṭūr: 19]. «البتَكُ» is cutting and splitting, and «البِتْكَةُ» is a piece of a thing, its plural being «بِتَك»:
165 - 2- حتى إذا ما هَوَتْ كَفُّ الغلام لها ... طارَتْ وفي كفِّه مِنْ ريشها بِتَكُ
(Until, when the boy's palm swooped down on it, it flew off, and in his hand were pieces of its feathers.)
The meaning of that is that the people of the Jāhiliyya used to slit the ear of the she-camel when she had given birth to five times, the last being a male.

semin-durr:120-120.t: And {يَعِدُهُمْ} was read with sukūn on the dāl for lightness, because of the succession of vowels; the object of the promise is omitted, i.e. "he promises them falsehood" or "safety and well-being". {إِلاَّ غُرُوراً} may be a second object, may be an object of purpose, may be an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, i.e. "a promise possessing deception", and may be a maṣdar not of the verb's own root, because «يَعِدُهم» is equivalent to «يَغُرُّهم بوعدِه» ("he deceives them by his promise").

semin-durr:121-121.t:
And {عَنْهَا}: it may be attached to an omitted word: either as a ḥāl from «محِيصاً», because in origin it is an adjective of an indefinite noun that was put before it, or as an explication, i.e. "I mean, from it"; and it is not permissible that it be attached to an omitted word, because it is not made transitive by «عن», nor to «محيصاً», even though the meaning is on that basis, because a maṣdar's object does not precede it; and whoever allows that allows «عن» being attached to it. «المحيص» is a noun of the maṣdar (ism maṣdar) of «حاصَ يَحِيص», when he got free and escaped; and it was said: it is turning aside in aversion, and from it is his saying:
165 - 3- ولم نَدْرِ إنْ حِصْناً من الموت حَيْصَةً ... كم العمرُ باقٍ والمَدَى مُتَطاوِلُ
(We did not know, if we turned away from death in flight, how much of life remains, though the span is long.)
And it is narrated: «جِضْنا» with jīm and ḍād, and from it: «وقعوا في حَيْصَ بَيْصَ» and «حاصَ باصَ», i.e. they fell into an affair from which it is hard to be free. One says «مَحِيص» and «مَحاص». He said:
165 - 4- أتَحِيصُ من حُكْمِ المَنِيَّةِ جاهداً ... ما للرجال عن المَنونِ مَحاصُ
(Do you strive to flee the judgement of fate? Men have no escape from death.)
One says: «حاصَ يَحُوص حَوْصاً وحِياصاً», i.e. he left the place in which he was; and «الحَوْصُ» is narrowness of the corner of the eye, and from it is «الأحْوَصُ».

semin-durr:122-122.t: And His saying the Exalted: {والذين آمَنُواْ}: it has two possibilities: the nominative as a mubtadaʾ with the khabar «سَنُدْخِلُهم», and the accusative by preoccupation (ishtighāl), i.e. "We shall admit those who believed, We shall admit them". «سيُدْخِلُهم» with the yāʾ of the third person was also read. «وعد الله» is accusative as a maṣdar of emphasis of itself (muʾakkid li-nafsihi), and «حقاً» as a maṣdar of emphasis of something other than itself (muʾakkid li-ghayrihi): «وعدَ» emphasises His saying «سندخلهم», and it is understood from what precedes it, and «حقاً» emphasises His saying {وَعْدَ الله}; and «قيلا» is accusative as a tamyīz. «القيل», «القول» and «القال» are maṣdars of one meaning, and from it is His saying the Exalted: {وَقِيلِهِ يارب} [al-Zukhruf: 88].

semin-durr:123-123.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {لَّيْسَ بِأَمَانِيِّكُمْ}: in «ليس» there is a pronoun which is its subject, and there is disagreement about it: it was said that it refers to something expressed; it was said that it refers to what the wording indicates of the verb; and it was said that the cause of the verse indicates it. As for its referring to something expressed, it was said that it is the promise given earlier in His saying {وَعْدَ الله}, and this is what al-Zamakhsharī chose; he said: "In «ليس» is the pronoun of the promise of Allah, i.e. what Allah promised of reward is not attained by your wishes nor by the wishes of the People of the Book. The address is to the Muslims, because none believes in the promise of Allah except one who believes in Him." And this is a good possibility. As for its referring to what the wording indicates, it was said that it is the faith understood from His saying «والذين آمنوا», and this is the view of al-Ḥasan, who said: "Faith is not by wishing." As for its referring to what the cause indicates, it was said that it refers to the boasting of the Muslims with the People of the Book, in that some of them said: "Our religion is before your religion, and our prophet is before your prophet, so we are better"; and the Muslims said: "Our Book judges over your Book, and our Prophet is the seal of the prophets"; so it was revealed. It was also said: it refers to the reward and punishment, i.e. neither reward for good deeds nor punishment for bad deeds is by your wishes. It was also said: the Jews said "We are the children of Allah and His beloved ones, and we are the people of Paradise", and likewise the Christians; and the disbelievers of Quraysh said "We shall not be resurrected", so it was revealed, i.e. what you claimed, O disbelievers of Quraysh, is not by your wishes.
Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, Shayba ibn Niṣāḥ, al-Ḥakam and al-Aʿraj read «أمانِيكم» and «ولا أمانِي» with lightening (a single yāʾ), as though they pluralised it on faʿālil rather than faʿālīl, as they said «قَرْقور» with plural «قراقير» and «قراقِر»; and the Arabs reduce the yāʾ from faʿālīl, just as they add it to faʿālil, as in the saying:
165 - 5-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . . . . . . . . . تَنْقادَ الصياريفِ
(... as the money-changers examine [coins].)
[Translator's note: the verse is quoted in the source only in part.] And His saying: {مَن يَعْمَلْ}: a resumptive clause that corroborates the ruling of the preceding clause. The majority read «ولا يَجِدْ» jussive, conjoined to the apodosis of the condition; it is narrated from Ibn ʿĀmir that it is nominative, which is by cutting off from the sequence. It may then be resumptive and it may be a ḥāl, so it was said, and there is a consideration in this, in that an imperfect negated by «لا» is not accompanied by the wāw when it occurs as a ḥāl.
His saying: {مِنَ الصالحات مِن ذَكَرٍ}: the first «من» is partitive, because the one under obligation cannot bear the doing of all righteous deeds. Al-Ṭabarī said: "It is redundant according to some", and there is weakness in this for the absence of the two conditions. And the second «مِنْ» is explicative. Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed it to be a ḥāl, and as to its owner there are two possibilities: the first, that it is the nominative pronoun of «يعمل»; the second, that it is «الصالحات», i.e. "righteous deeds, from male or female"; the clarification of this has already been given at His saying: {لاَ أُضِيعُ عَمَلَ عَامِلٍ مِّنْكُمْ مِّن ذَكَرٍ أَوْ أنثى} [Āl ʿImrān: 195], and the discussion on «أو» too. And His saying «وهو مؤمن» is a circumstantial clause from the agent of «يعمل». Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read «يُدْخَلون» here, in Maryam and at the beginning of Ghāfir, with ḍamma on the imperfect prefix and fatḥa on the khāʾ, passive; Ibn Kathīr and Abū Bakr alone for the second in Ghāfir, and Abū ʿAmr alone for the one in Fāṭir; the rest read it with fatḥa on the imperfect prefix and ḍamma on the khāʾ, active, and that is for variety in eloquence, and differences may be apparent that this book cannot accommodate.
